author: José Saramago
introFa: کتاب «Seeing» نوشته José Saramago یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C1 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Seeing»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

BOOK REVIEWS 66 1 Robert J. Nelson Seeing Through Words , Seeing Through W ords , Seeing W >rds Through , Seeing IV ords ( 'as ) Through * In post-structuralist thought the object of study has become the study of study. The model not its representations, the paradigm not its cases, the set not its examples, the program not its features, the law not the canon- these are the ruling concerns of inquiry in the most serious "departments" of inquiry into nature and thought, in the humanities as in science (physical and social). Looking at the phenomenon with an historical perspective that is not, in Lovejoy's term, "presenticentric"- the "natural philosophy" of Greco/Roman antiquity, say, reprised during the European Renaissance, which considered science and the "humanities" in a continuum as objects of inquiry- some would claim that models, paradigms, sets, programs, laws have always been the ruling concerns of science , of inquiry into any aspect of nature or thought. Yet, if it seems always to have been so- indeed: to have to have been so- to scientists of nature and thought , for most humanists after the European Renaissance, a different "model" or inquiry into the "thought" of the arts (and especially of the art of words that we call Literature) ob- tained. In this model, science and literature were differentiated with respect to both objects of inquiry and modes of inquiry into the differing objects. The differentiation was made along an epistemological axis: science dealt with (nonhuman) "nature," art or the humanities with "thought"- which is to say, "human nature." Nevertheless, a common "moral" perspective guided each inquiry: small-й humanism (the discovery of nature and the retrieval of thought) subserved capital-й Humanism in a "humanitarian" perspective that ordered (arranged and ordained) the discovered and retrieved objects and the understanding of their relations to one another in their separate spheres of inquiry for the "benefit of mankind." In the scientific study of nature and in the humanistic study of thought the underlying assumption was that the objects were bound in themselves rather than by introjection * An essay-review of American Hieroglyphics: The Symbol of the Egyptian Hieroglyphics in the Ameri- can Renaissance. By John T. Irwin. New Haven: Yale University Press, 1980. xii, 371 pp. $19.50. All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

66 2 THE GEORGIA REVIEW of the inquirer's bias to yield this benefit. This, so it seemed to the inquirers, was the nature of both nature and thought- especially so to the inquirers into thought, for whom the "dark ages" had aborted the "birth of thought" in Greco/Roman antiquity. Understandably, they regarded their new beginning as a rebirth, a Renaissance. These familiar perspectives make of the "American Renaissance," as re- assessed by John T. Irwin in his fascinating new book, a gloomy paradox. Rooting his reassessment of Emerson, Thoreau, Poe, Hawthorne, Melville, and Whitman in the French archaeologist Champollion's interpretation of Egyptian hieroglyphics with the aid of the bilingual text of the Rosetta Stone, Irwin traces a reprise of the perspectives of "natural philosophy" in the work of these artists / humanists of nineteenth-century America. Their Renaissance begins, well enough, in Emerson and Thoreau and Whitman, with a recon- structive optimism not unlike that of the scientists and humanists of the first Renaissance; but almost as soon in Poe and Hawthorne (and eventually in Melville) it seems to issue in a deconstruction of the dualistic epistemology and humanitarian, perfectibilitarian ethics of the first Renaissance. The "deconstruction," as the word will have alerted my readers, emerges through the reflection on language that is a central concern of all these writers: the reconstructionist Emerson, Thoreau, and Whitman, as well as the deconstructionist (in Irwin's view) Poe, Hawthorne, and Melville. Like the room or space for Oedipal revolt that Harold Bloom traces in the his- tory of poetry, the ground of language-as-and-for-meaning that Irwin traces in these writers shrinks entropically. Indeed, in Irwin's history, it is the third rather than the second law of thermodynamics j that is at work, 7 with zero- j 7 point energy- the point at which language self-destructs or self-deconstructs -being reached finally in Melville. In my opinion, however, the case is not everywhere so convincing as Irwin makes it. If Melville in The Confidence-Man "is out to sharp those unselfconscious readers who, like the old man with the counterfeit detector, are so intent on seeing through the words that they never see through the words" (p. 335), Emerson and Thoreau- as Irwin brings out- are intent on proving that we see not only through but in words the world itself: As a metaphysical interpreter, Emerson identifies the simple and the necessary with the hidden, with that which is beneath the obvious surface of things. If in studying history one under- stands that "it is the spirit and not the fact that is identical," then everyday experience will always be "verifying some pre- diction to us and converting into things the words and signs which we had heard and seen without heed." That is, under the impulse of metaphysical insight, the arbitrary language of con- vention ("words and signs") will be penetrated to reveal once more the necessary, emblematic language of nature ("things") from which it sprang, (p. 10) All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

BOOK REVIEWS 663 Even more so for Thoreau. Noting that "the basic form that unites the ani- mal body and the vegetable leaf is, for Thoreau, the lobe or drop" (p. 16), Irwin goes on to trace Thoreau's lessons in "creative etymology" (e.g., on "leaf" in both Greek and English, where the order of consonants iterates the thawing of a sandbank described by Thoreau, as well as on "lobe" and "globe," pp. 17-19) and concludes: Having penetrated the emblematic world of natural forms to discover the inner, unifying form, and then having presented as an analogue of this process the penetration of the language of convention to discover the original language of nature in which words are emblems of things, Thoreau concludes: "Thus it seemed that this one hillside illustrated the principle of all the operations of Nature. The Maker of this earth but patented a leaf. What Champollion will decipher this hieroglyphic for us, that we may turn over a new leaf at last?" The answer to that question is, obviously, Thoreau himself, (p. 19) As Irwin himself cogently brings out on the basis of his wide-ranging review of the impact of Champollion's researches on American philosophy and theology of the early nineteenth century, Emerson and Thoreau have opted for that interpretation of Egyptian hieroglyphics which posits the precedence of the pictographic over the phonetic, in Derridian terms of the priority of speech over writing.* They are compelled to do so, in Irwin's opinion, because of the consonance they see (in the corruption of God's "Word") between Man's postlapsarian state of sin and human language. In their flight from the abstraction of language (in speech or writing)- an ab- straction which is itself part or sign of the corruption- they would restore the original unity of man with and in God through the demonstration of the emblematic or pictographic character of language itself. Irwin does not raise, as a Pascal might in view of this conception, the theological issue of the human presumption that this linguistics implies. But, then, neither do Emer- son and Thoreau. Whitman's "omnigenous" linguistics is of a piece with but ultimately overreaches the epistemological notions of Emerson and Thoreau. Where Emerson and Thoreau looked to the "book" of nature in search of its (their) "inmost leaf," Whitman extends the pictographic/phonetic polarity (and, thus theologically, the debate) emerging from Champollion and other re- * It is of interest to note that, unlike most deconstructionists with their privileging of intertextuality, Irwin does not shy away from that (to them) hoary category of "tra- ditional" literary scholarship: influence. Nor, for that matter, does he develop, either explicitly or implicitly, the notion of an intertextual (really: intratextual) sameness or even similarity between the major writers he considers. They do not all come to the same thing: hieroglyphically, the pictographic/speechifying Emerson, Thoreau, Whit- man stand against the phonetic/scriptifying Poe, Hawthorne, Melville. Moreover, within each pole, there is a progression, although (as my earlier comparison between Irwin and Bloom indicates) in the case of the scriptors we must really speak of a degression. 664 THE GEORGIA REVIEW searchers. As Irwin brings out through an admirable erudition based on original sources, Whitman had reliable reports on as well as, at times, first- hand knowledge of these sources. For the great bard: The poetic transformation of the physical into the metaphysi- cal is synonymous with the attempt to recapture the original language of objects, for in that language physical objects were, to use Emerson's term, "transparent," their significances shone through their material shapes. Physical objects were transpar- ently metaphysical objects, signs in which no separation or discontinuity between form and content existed because as pic- tographic ideograms their form was their content. Whitman's attempt to regain the original language of natural signs, his effort to replace "audible words" with "the presentation of the unspoken meanings of the earth," involves the paradoxical use of phonetic signs to restore the unspoken (nonphonetic) lan- guage of pictographic ideograms, the paradox involved in sing- ing "the songs of the body ." (p. 38) For Whitman, singing is signing- the supreme if not only way, as Irwin observes, of transcending "the mediation of spoken language through the mediation of spoken language," the way in which "Whitman's effort to transform the physical into the metaphysical must be understood" (p. 38). The song of himself, the reconstructive self -reflexi vity, that is Whit- man's poetry would have been for Poe, according to Irwin, a vanity of vanities. With Poe (to whom Irwin devotes more than half of his book) begins a perplexed self-reflectivity that is, for Irwin, only the threshold of the fictional house of Hawthorne with its gloomy gable windows looking out ambiguously on the deconstructive reflection of endless sea in the port- holes of Melville's fiction. Irwin's look-see into the world and word of pond and brook in Thoreau becomes a seeing through to the very end of wilderness-world and word in Hawthorne and the sea-world and sea-word of Poe and Melville. In this sea-word voyage Irwin concentrates, not sur- prisingly, on Poe's work dealing with voyages: stories, finished and un- finished, and the writer's scholarly reflections on linguistics and especially hieroglyphics as well as original sources for these essays and fictions. The lead-ship in Irwin's voyage into Poe's linguistic voyages is the Nar- rative of A. Gordon Рут . Irwin takes us on a voyage of learning and inter- pretation as extraordinary as Pym-Poe's, with numerous ports of call but notably at Wilhelm and especially Alexander von Humboldt to provide "structuralist" doubts on Emerson's and Thoreau's pictographic interpreta- tion of hieroglyphics; ancient (Ptolemy Hephestion) and modern (Lewis and Clark as well as other commentators on their voyages, among them Poe) geographers and explorers to illustrate that the abysses, whirlpools, vortices, auras, mists, undifferentiated expanses of black or of white that all such voyagers encounter in their quest of origin (of man, of language, of mean- ing) are but anticipations and confirmations of Pym-Poe's narrative counter- All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

BOOK REVIEWS 665 statement to the assertion by Poe in Eureka that "nothing is, or can be, su- perior to any one soul- that each soul is, in part, its own God- its own Creator" (quoted by Irwin, p. 225). However, writes Irwin, If Poe's deification of human consciousness to save it from an annihilating return to oneness is, in our tradition, logically im- plicit in that prior deification of consciousness (its presence ab origine) in Genesis, then Poe's assertion that man, in his return to origin, will "recognize his existence as that of Je- hovah" need not be interpreted as an unqualified prophecy of some ultimate cosmic consciousness. Rather, the assertion can be seen as one pole of an opposition between belief and doubt whose other pole is the ending of Рут with its skeptical sense of what it means to recognize the self as God. By interpreting the misty figure with its aura of divinity as Pym's unrecognized shadow, the reader recognizes/acknowledges that "God" has always been a self-projected, idea-lized [sic] image of man, a personification of man's alogical desire for a form of conscious- ness released from the constraints of the body, time, and death, made omniscient and ubiquitous, primordially creative and eternally existent, (p. 226) The doubt that is cast narratively upon the assertion of "mind (really, iw'W, as Irwin stresses) over matter" is buttressed by other features of the nar- rative, notably the linguistic play between the regions of "Tsalal" where all is black and "Tekeli-li" where all is white. Irwin does some of his most scrupulous and inventive scholarship in exploring the roots of these names, tracing their etymons in Ethiopie, Hebrew, and Arabic forms ("hiero- glyphically," of course) to conjecture that "if the ultimate root of Tsalal is si (shadow) and that of its polar opposite Tekeli-li is tkl (original, fixed spot), then together the origins of the two words are a hieroglyph of the final scene in Рут- the shadow at the pole- a pictograph of that shadowing or doubling that is the origin of the bipolar oppositions of the linguistic world" (pp. 2 3 2~ 3 3 ) - Helpful as Irwin's research is here, one is puzzled that he did not con- sider the onomatopoeic hoaxing that, for all its humor, actually supports Irwin's (and, presumably, Poe's) sure etymologizing here. In itself, Tsalal, spoken phonetically can be " 'tis all all" and might as easily be applied to white as to black ("it's all black" or "it's all white"), with the repetition of the "al" an index to the expanse of the color in question. However, when one plays the same phonetic hoax with the declared opposite of Tsalal, the region of Tekeli-li, where all is white as in "Take a (hard a as in take ) lily," one can, by the very linguistic bipolarity Irwin traces more eruditely through the linguistic roots, conclude that the "al" in the first region is a "black all." Similarly, one wonders at other hesitations on Irwin's part that may not have been Poe's own: Pym may be Poe's (more cryptically learned) hoax on (a) pimenta , "a genus of tropical American aromatic trees having large All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

666 THE GEORGIA REVIEW coriaceous leaves" ( Webster's New Third International Dictionary ), thereby an allusion to Poe's own Southern roots as well as, through the association of leaf and inscription, to his status as a writer; ( b ) piment or pyment "an aromatic spice or a wine flavored with spice and honey," whereby Poe may have been pointing to the kind of hieroglyphic doubling (bitter or sharp/ sweet) that is Irwin's concern throughout his book; ( с ) pigment , "a natural or synthetic inorganic or organic substance that imparts a color including black or white to other materials," thereby, once again and more closely to Poe's (and Irwin's) concerns with writing, a veiled allusion to the Poe(t), author of Рут , the narrative by a man whose own name at the level of phonetic hoaxing by assonance only reenforces these (possible) learned etymologies: pym-pin-pen. Irwin demonstrates both the same capacity for learning shrewdly ap- plied and reticence before possible if not probable phonetic hi (ero) -jinks in support of that application in his sections on Hawthorne. The ambivalence created by the play or text (-ure- that is, sentence or phrase) with narrative (structure) in Poe becomes, in Hawthorne, an ambiguity of text(ure) and structure. Though he takes account of the whole canon, Irwin concentrates on what is for him its most emblematic moment, The Scarlet Letter , to signalize Hawthorne's doubt, so deconstructive of the sense of self where Descartes' was so (re)constructive of that very sense. Thus, As Dimmesdale looks at the "tapestried comfort of the walls" and then at his unfinished manuscript, Hawthorne encourages the reader to equate the pictograph embroidered on the veil and its revelation of Dimmesdale's double role with the phonetic script of Dimmesdale's text and its manifestation of his divided self. The internally split/ externally doubled terms of this equa- tion are Hawthorne's means of questioning the symbolist effort to make opaque phonetic script achieve a force of expression equivalent to the necessary transparency of a pictograph. For Hawthorne implies that a pictograph's transparency is simply the uncertain, illusory transparency of a mirror image, (p. 258) Shedding deliberately blinding, confusing light on The Scarlet Letter is Hawthorne's sketch, "Monsieur du Miroir," where "Hawthorne's own sub- jectivity is the subject of his writing" (p. 263). Veiled subject and veiled subjectivity: the author of the prefatory "Custom House" of the great novel veils his allusions to his business- and church-minded ancestors, the Hathornes, the very addition of a "i¿?" to his own ancestral name being a part of that veil; he further veils the very tale "he" will tell by attributing to a Jonathan Pue the manuscript of the tale, which, as Irwin writes penetratingly, "con- fronts Hawthorne with the image of a previous surveyor who had also been an author, confronts him at precisely the moment when Hawthorne feels that he himself 'had ceased to be a writer of tolerably poor tales and essays, and had become a tolerably good Surveyor of the Customs' " (p. 277). These and other veils of the novel are not all that transparent, of course, and it is to All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

BOOK REVIEWS 667 Irwin's credit that he penetrates to their polyvalent and mystifying impact on the reader: the Oedipal revolt in the very change of his name in relation to the "serious" men-of-the-world-and-the-church who are his "fathers" (p. 276); the "A" itself which is never explicitly interpreted by the novelist as the mark of "adultery" but which is surely that and, as surely, the mark (name) of "Arthur" who is Dimmesdale and the "author" who is Haw- thorne (p. 283); the resuscitation of the long-dead Pue's manuscript through which Hawthorne, like Pue himself, will achieve "the kind of survival" in which "his public self must die so that his writing self can be reborn" (p. 278). One is here, as in his pages on Poe, puzzled by Irwin's not having ex- ploited more obvious decipherings. Given Hawthorne's artistic sensitivity and, relatedly, his feminism- especially as both are perceptively and movingly interpreted in Oedipal terms by Irwin- might not the 'W he added to his name stand for "woman"? Again, Dimmesdale is possibly "dimmest dale," the character signifying in his very name that play of the shadow of the valley of death, of this vale of tears that is human existence; Jonathan Pue is possibly, in his first name, an allusion to (a) the son of Saul who, though in line to his father's throne, yet protects David, anointed by God to succeed to Saul's throne, even as Jonathan Pue, "protects" David/Nathaniel that he may succeed as artist instead of businessman to the glory of the kingdom as his ancestors cannot, for, like Saul, they tolerate idol worship (of commerce); or ( b ) an allusion to the scribe in whose house the prophet Jeremiah was a prisoner, even as the prophet Hawthorne is a prisoner in the house of the scribe, Jonathan Pue. In his second name, Pue is possibly (a) that ecclesiastical piece of furniture where we sit and kneel (pue, archaic of pew) in supplica- tion and adoration of God or ( b ) that balcony or podium (pew from Latin podia , plural of podium ), an etymology obviously connected to (a) above but which, in its secular development into podium , might be the podium from which Hawthorne will speak. In both (a) and ( b ) here, of course, the further etymological connection with Greek podion , "small foot, base," sug- gests the ambiguous reversal of usual narrative order: the base stands upon the building, the "preface" is the "tale," Hawthorne's preface is but a preface to a preface. However, through the identification between Pue and Haw- thorne we can see that the narrative reversal is a paradoxical structure in which Hawthorne is Pue; preface by Hawthorne and tale by Pue are one. There is, of course, a third possible etymon of Pue: "pue" as an exclamation of olfactory dissatisfaction, as in French puer , "to smell, to stink." Pue's is a tale stinking of shame, deceit, betrayal, filth. In keeping with Irwin's hy- pothesis of ambiguity in (of ) Hawthorne, particularly with respect to words, I suggest that Hawthorne may have both the phonetic (Biblical) and the pictographic (olfactory) meanings in mind, thereby offering a further am- biguity to those " 'few who will understand him' " (quoted by Irwin, p. 267). Indeed, Irwin's emphasis on ambiguity is even greater in his pages on Melville: "In Pierre, Melville represents this double ambiguity of physical nature and the self as that of reciprocal texts"; "trapped in this circular, reciprocal ambiguity, Ahab . . (both on p. 288); "And if we prejudge him All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

668 THE GEORGIA REVIEW [Frank Goodman of The Confidence-Man ], won't that determine our inter- pretation of the subsequent ambiguous evidence?" (p. 331). As my quota- tions indicate, the focus of Irwin's pages on Melville (pp. 285-349) is broader, with many works getting sustained attention (with Billy Budd getting none, however, a point to which I shall return) but Pierre , Moby -Dick, Mardi and The Confidence- Man the most sustained. For all the emphasis on ambiguity in Hawthorne (particularly through the concept of the mirror), for Hawthorne himself the mirrors do not con- stitute a crazifying maze: "Humorously imagining himself as an original, as a living source in their midst (the town pump), Hawthorne obliquely ex- presses his desire that the book- the phallic shadow/child, the partial object of the imagination- will perpetuate him from generation to generation, will be a 'living hieroglyphic,' its meaning and destiny as vitally indeterminate as his own" (p. 284, emphasis added). The mirror-autograph of "Monsieur du Miroir," like the Pue manuscript, is really a two-way mirror: behind the reflecting surface Hawthorne stands in the "real world," from which he looks through the reflecting surfaces of both Pue as author of the manuscript and Hawthorne as author of the preface to see that all three are one, that the two reflections are drawn back into his own identity. No such "reconstruction" of self and /in reality "is possible in Melville, for the indeterminacy or "indefiniteness" that results from Melville's reading of "reality" and "self" as well as from our reading of Melville is anything but "vital." I cull along this sememic axis from Irwin's pages on Melville: That indeterminacy is the essential characteristic of the hiero- glyph for Melville is made clear in Ishmael's discussion of the whiteness of the whale, (p. 286) . . . And we understand that the hieroglyph of the world is doubly undecipherable. It is indefinite in itself, and in its indefi- niteness it allows the individual subject to project onto it the structure of a self as undecipherable as the world, (p. 288) . . . The novel's [The Confidence-Man ] apocalypse ( apo , "from," plus kalyptein , "to veil"), its concluding revelation, concerns the original indeterminacy of self-consciousness, the apocryphal (apo, "away," plus kryptein , "to hide") nature of symbolization and the knowledge it provides, (pp. 345-46) As Irwin evokes the double and contradictory meaning of the Greek prefix, apo ("from" or "of" in a genitive sense, "away" or "asunder" in an ablative sense), one is tempted to read Melville's canon not genitively as an Apologia pro vita sua in the manner of his great contemporary Cardinal Newman, but ablatively as an "apology" through words that tells us that words are through . Yet, does not the narrative (sequence of events) give pause to this radical deconstructionist interpretation of the texture (the assertions of words and sentences)? In the texts of the canon he has examined, Irwin might reply "not at all!" This is the very brunt of Irwin's workmanlike examination of All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

BOOK REVIEWS 669 sequencing and sentencing in Mardi and, especially, The Confidence-Man . However, for all the attentiveness he showed earlier to the philosophic im- plications of the narrative even in Poe and Hawthorne, here Irwin seems so bent on the sememic and lexemic that he fails at least to consider the pos- sibility that narrative may have an ironic effect on texture. The galled tongue (instrument of speech) that Irwin finds in Mardi , Pierre , and The Confidence- Man may be in Melville's cheek. All of Melville's readers may not be so literate or so literal as Irwin as they watch and hear Frank Goodman and Charlie Noble "con" each other. Some readers (including, possibly, Melville himself as he writes these "hieroglyphical" texts) may be like Daniel J. Boorstin in the "Foreword" to his 1964 book, The Image: A Guide to Pseudo- events in America-. "One need not be a doctor to know he is sick, nor a shoemaker to feel the shoe pinch. I do not know what 'reality' really is. But somehow I do know an illusion when I see one " (p. iii, emphasis added). Boorstin's "somehow" may strike Irwin as an arbitrary and naïve vestige of an unsophisticated linguistics. Yet, it has a long tradition in debates about language, at least as old as that seventeenth century in which Irwin finds that "questions that had once been defined as metaphysical . . . had been reinterpreted as epistemological." The reinterpretation of these "epistemo- logica!" questions as "linguistic questions" that Irwin finds "just beginning ... in the nineteenth century" (p. 318) had actually begun at least in the debate between Descartes and Pascal. From his basically Derridian-de Manian perspective, Irwin chides Descartes: What more basic ground than sense experience could we fall back on to provide the referent for the word? All that one could appeal to would be an inner feeling or intuition, a purely subjective state, as when Descartes, unable to verify the real existence of external objects, falls back upon the thinking sub- ject's certainty of its own existence. Yet the difficulty is that subject and object, as reciprocal opposites, cannot be wholly separated. There cannot be a purely subjective state. . . . Des- cartes' "I think, therefore I am" as an example of certain knowledge already assumes that the subject is certain that he is thinking as opposed to dreaming or hallucinating, yet the dif- ferentiation of thinking from other subjective states depends upon an implicit privileging of waking consciousness (and its various modes of testing) as the norm, just as that notion of stable, certain being which Descartes affirms of the thinking subject derives its meaning from the being of waking con- sciousness. (pp. 256-57) This reading of Descartes is curiously commonplace in view of Irwin's scrupulous erudition on so many figures in the history of thought whom he evokes. Half a century ago (Paris, 1925) in the commentary to his masterful edition of Le Discours de la méthode , Etienne Gilson demonstrated that the "ergo" (therefore) of the cogito is really a coordinate not a causal conjunc- tion: "I think and I am." Nevertheless, it is true that Descartes as much as All use subject to JSTOR Terms and Conditions

670 THE GEORGIA REVIEW the Egyptologizing authors of the American Renaissance was involved in a relentless pursuit of the origins of world, word, and self. The simultaneity of thought and being that Gilson finds to be Descartes' epistemology does, indeed, make an abstraction of the senses; but contrary to Irwin's assumption (that "the subject is certain that he is thinking as opposed to dreaming or hallucinating"), Descartes assumes that it is God who guarantees the differ- ence between waking and dreaming (see the concluding paragraphs of the Fourth Part of The Discourse on Method ). "Assumes" rather than "posits" (as Irwin might read this act), for the act is psychological rather than epistemological. Descartes comes to this psychological ground of knowing after an earlier search, in the Regulae ad directionem ingenii (1628), for an epistemological ground. In that earlier text he shows that sin of "angelism" that Jacques Maritain has attributed to him: the desire to find the first prin- ciple, the very root of thinking, such that he will have not only discovered the principle itself but will, like God, control or have present to his mind every link of a chain of reasoning. Descartes is a much more desperate figure than Irwin's invocation of him suggests. Certainly Descartes was a desperate and ridiculous figure as far as his contemporary Pascal was concerned. To Descartes' dualism, as to his regres- sive pursuit of the first principle, Pascal gives more than the "pshaw" that deconstructionists might give to Boorstin's appeal to the pinch of the shoe. For Pascal, one has no need of a first principle , since nature has given us an epistemological (and psychological) floor or ground from which to de- cide when we are awake or when we are sleeping: the ground of a "first sentiment ." The sentiment is Augustinián rather than Lockean, of course; it is rife with both the feeling of pain and the pain of feeling. Nor is the nature to which Pascal appeals for this ground itself grounded in God-as- Guarantor, whatever the illusions of thought (interpreting nature itself or other thought) be, including the matter of God and our relation to him as possible illusions ( The Thoughts , Sellier edition, Paris: Mercure de France, 1976, from fr. 681). Again, in his treatise On the Art of Persuasion (usually conjoined with his treatise On the Geometric Spirit ), Pascal- in implicit response to Descartes' regressive pursuit- stresses the notion of this "first sentiment" as the ground for human acts of perception (see especially the first three paragraphs). To be sure, Pascal is as aware as Melville of the "aporetic" (Louis Marin's term in his 1975 La Critique du discours : sur la "Logique de Fort Royal " et les " Pensées " de Pascal) potential of language; true, this "aporesis" of word and phrase is projected in an "unfinished" work, that masterpiece we call The Thoughts (in Pascal's project, really An Apology for the Christian Religion ). However, that the work is "unfinished" or "in- definite," does not mean, to borrow one of Irwin's most brilliant insights on Poe, that its structure or architecture is itself but a sign of the radically de- constructive nature of human symbolization. The play between aporetic or skeptical word-phrase of the fragments and the relatively finished (as the best modern editorial scholarship from Tourneur through Lafuma to Sellier indicates) structure provides the possibility of seeing that words may not be altogether through. This play be- tween text(ure) and structure in Pascal seems, as I have indicated, apposite in Melville. It is, of course, a play that is at once an interaction and a play- fulness of the kind that phrase- and word-bound deconstructionists may be incapable of seeing or, as the common root (OE secgan) indicates, saying . The playfulness emerges from that Latin root for both see and 1 vit ( videre ) via Greek eidenai, "to know ." Seeing is believing, as Pascal (and perhaps Derrida, in spite of himself) can testify, in a way that saying is not. It is a matter of the order of the heart. The heart is what is missing in Irwin's pages on Melville, as it is not in his emotionally as well as intellectually compelling pages on Hawthorne. Can this awareness of the heart be what compels Irwin to fail to take account of Billy Budd in his otherwise thorough review of the Melville canon that, he would have his readers believe, anticipates the deconstructionist lessons emerging from Paris and New Haven these days? The lesson of these lessons, hermeneutically, is that words indeed are through as "signifiers," for they are "but a sound and a fury, signifying nothing." Those who love language and literature as much as Melville and Irwin must shudder at the thought of what those without the rich erudition and obvious knowledge of Melville and Irwin will do with this lesson. Will those "literary" specialists for whom the only canon is the critical canon think that they do not have to read Billy Budd with its brooding and zmplayful articulation of text(ure) and structure? Perhaps Irwin felt it unnecessary to demonstrate that the grim dirge, "Billy in the Darbies," after which Melville writes "End of Book," obviously (in Irwin's view) takes back the dying Captain Vere's unremorseful last words: "Billy Budd, Billy Budd." Perhaps those unremorseful words are only con- firmed as signifiers of the meaninglessness, seen by Vere in his own life, to which the Billy of the dirge seems to testify in his descent into sleep (dream) as the "oozy weeds" twist about him. Perhaps. On the other hand, the ballad is really not Billy's. It is the work of another foretopman of "artless poetic temperament" who is as susceptible as the greatest scholar of misreading the hieroglyph of Billy's life; or of Claggert's, whose very physiognomy (or phrenology) posits the complexity of our efforts to signify our sentiments ; or of Captain Vere's, who "loved books" and who had "nothing of that literary taste which less heeds the thing conveyed than the vehicle," whose "bias was towards those books to which every serious mind of superior order occupying any active post of authority in the world, naturally inclines: books treating of actual men and events no matter of what era- history, biography, and unconventional writ- ers, who, free from cant and convention , like Montaigne , honestly and in the spirit of common sense philosophize from realities [ emphasis added]"; or of Melville himself who, in this his last major work, perhaps sees through the seeing-through of words as through . Such a construal depends, of course, on a much broader context for the text that is itself Irwin's almost exclusive focus. Yet as much as he broods about linguistic matters, Melville (like his confrères of the American Renais- sance, particularly Hawthorne and Whitman) broods as well about historical matters- the "ship of state," for example, as it is buffeted about emblemati- cally on seas of economic and political troubles. For Irwin, Moby -Dick is neither a whale of a story nor a story of a whale- it is the wail of story. For Irwin, the "fountain-whirlpool contains" even as it "overflows." Yet, might not Moby-Dick be as well Melville's ruminations on the socio-economic and political turmoil of Jacksonian Democracy with its land and bank crises, its "energy crisis"? Is it possible that Ahab, with his dictation of the union (the crew of the Pequod) in pursuit of the source of energy (the whale's sperm), is a pictograph for Andrew Jackson ("Old Hickory")- who in 1830 proclaimed, "Our Federal Union! It must and shall be preserved!"; who in- sisted on payment in specie during the banking crisis; and who gained much of his support from the workingmen of the East as well as from farmers of the West? Melville set sail for the first time (at age 20) just after the close of Jackson's second term (1837) on a five-year voyage, a year and a half of it (1841-42) on a whaler. Is Moby-Dick a cautionary tale about the "state of the union" as he found it in the Jacksonian and Post- Jacksonian era? Similarly, in Billy Budd, is Captain Vere (a hewer to truth) modeled on Abraham Lincoln, another hewer to first truths and union? Is the "Handsome Sailor," Billy Budd, the white (pictographic) soul of the black man (a pic- tograph of slavery), the first "Handsome Sailor" whom Melville evokes? Is Claggart, that clag ("a clot or lump, esp. of dirt or snow"), a pictograph of Southern culture which was democratic (snow) in all but slavery (dirt) according to Robert Penn Warren in his The Legacy of the Civil War (1964) ? As Irwin's penetrating pages on the hold of phrenology in nineteenth- century America give grounds to believe, Claggart's "features . . . cleanly cut as those of a Greek medallion" may be the very sign of that democracy, spoiled as was Greek democracy by its chin (lower part) with its "strange protuberant heaviness," the pictographic hieroglyphic, we might say with Emerson and Thoreau, of the guilty burden of slavery. Such construais with reference to "actual men and events" bring Mel- ville closer to his own Captain Vere than to Irwin's models in Paris and New Haven with respect to Melville's or any reader's ruminations about sym- bolization. They also bring him closer to Captain Vere's model, Montaigne.
